JP.nov: Autumn foliage and cool city walks shape November trips across much of Japan. Kyoto can be busy near peak colour; northern and mountain areas are colder.
JP.dec: Winter illuminations and the opening ski season become travel themes. Snow and temperatures vary by region. Year-end holidays bring busy travel and some business closures.

TH.nov: Cooler, generally drier weather supports northern cultural trips and Andaman coast holidays. The Gulf islands have a different rainfall pattern and can still be very wet.
TH.dec: Inland Thailand remains in its popular cool season, with cooler mountain nights. Andaman beach travel is in season; Gulf-coast rainfall still requires checking local conditions.

AU.nov: November is spring across temperate Australia, suitable for varied outdoor itineraries. Tropical northern regions enter their wet season, so a nationwide beach-weather assumption would mislead.
AU.dec: Summer begins in the temperate south, supporting coastal and outdoor trips. The tropical north remains in its wet season; regional conditions matter more than a national average.

NZ.nov: Late spring offers nature-focused itineraries before summer. Match outdoor plans to local conditions and allow flexibility; New Zealand's mountains and coasts do not share one climate.
NZ.dec: December starts summer, when beaches and outdoor experiences feature strongly. The tourism board identifies December to February as the summer season; this is seasonal guidance, not measured demand.

AE.nov: Dubai's cooler-season calendar supports beach visits, desert excursions and outdoor dining. This regional example does not describe every emirate or establish a ranking of visitor origins.
AE.dec: Outdoor attractions, festive markets and year-end celebrations are central Dubai themes. Pleasant winter conditions support open-air itineraries; event dates and individual programmes still need separate confirmation.

QA.nov: Qatar's winter season starts in November, bringing milder conditions for souq visits, parks, waterfront walks and desert activities. These are general seasonal conditions rather than a forecast.
QA.dec: Mild daytime weather and cooler evenings favour outdoor cultural and coastal experiences. Pack for changing evening temperatures and check short-term conditions before desert or sea excursions.

ZA.nov: Cape Town moves from spring toward its sunny summer, with outdoor and food events. South Africa's regional climates differ, so safari and coastal itineraries need separate planning.
ZA.dec: Cape Town's warm summer supports beaches, gardens and outdoor performances. December is a popular visiting period there; other regions have different rainfall patterns and travel conditions.

IN.nov: Delhi's autumn generally supports sightseeing with lighter layers than midwinter. Diwali and Rajasthan's fairs add cultural interest in 2026. Conditions vary widely across India's regions.
IN.dec: Northern cities become cooler while Himalayan destinations can face snow and access constraints. Delhi and Himachal illustrate different winter experiences; a single national weather label is inappropriate.

DE.nov: Late November brings the opening of many Christmas markets. Berlin illustrates the shift toward illuminated squares, seasonal shopping and cultural city breaks; openings differ by venue.
DE.dec: Christmas markets, light displays and performances shape urban itineraries. Check each market's operating days and closing date, especially near Christmas, rather than assuming uninterrupted daily opening.

AT.nov: Many Austrian Christmas markets start during the second half of November. Alpine ski openings begin selectively, with operating dates dependent on snow, altitude and resort decisions.
AT.dec: Advent markets and skiing are complementary travel themes. Most resorts target late-November to mid-December openings, but planned dates remain conditional on weather and snow conditions.

FI.nov: Christmas markets begin to add seasonal interest, while Lapland's Santa experiences operate beyond Christmas itself. Build itineraries around local opening schedules and actual winter conditions.
FI.dec: Christmas traditions, sauna and winter outdoor activities shape trips. Rovaniemi offers Santa experiences; snow-based activities should be checked locally because conditions and availability vary by place.

NO.nov: Northern Norway moves toward polar night from mid-November. Long dark evenings suit aurora watching when skies permit, while daylight and winter conditions differ greatly by latitude.
NO.dec: Short days and northern polar night define many winter itineraries. Aurora sightings depend on conditions; choose activities and transport for the specific destination, rather than expecting guaranteed lights.

ES.nov: Autumn food, forests and rural trips feature in Spain's monthly travel guidance. Extremadura's Ambroz valley is one example, while Christmas lights begin arriving toward month end.
ES.dec: City lights, nativity scenes and Christmas markets become prominent. Madrid's New Year's Eve grape tradition is a seasonal highlight; the Canary Islands offer a different winter setting.

IT.nov: Autumn itineraries emphasise villages, countryside and regional food. Alba's truffle fair adds a dated 2026 attraction; foliage and harvest experiences depend on region and timing.
IT.dec: Christmas-decorated cities, markets and mountain holidays shape winter trips. Italy's national tourism board highlights places from Bolzano to Rome; ski conditions need separate local checks.

SG.nov: Singapore stays warm and humid. November's inter-monsoon period often brings afternoon or evening thunderstorms, so combine outdoor neighbourhood walks with flexible indoor options and rain breaks.
SG.dec: The Northeast Monsoon's wet phase can bring extended rain spells. Festive city experiences remain possible, but outdoor schedules should be flexible; climate normals are not a daily forecast.

MA.nov: Autumn is highlighted by Morocco's tourism board for Sahara trips. Coastal, inland and mountain conditions differ, so avoid applying a Marrakech or desert description to the whole country.
MA.dec: Coasts can be comparatively mild while mountain winters are cold and wet. Plan clothing and transport around altitude and route, with local checks for mountain access and conditions.

VN.nov: Vietnam needs regional planning rather than a single national season. Central-coast rain can affect itineraries; consult local conditions when combining northern, central and southern destinations.
VN.dec: The national tourism guide highlights Phu Quoc for tropical beach trips. Northern Vietnam is cooler, while central destinations can remain wet; choose regions to match the desired experience.

CA.nov: Holiday lights brighten cities as the season turns toward winter. Ontario's urban and regional routes offer one example; Canada-wide conditions vary substantially, especially for snow-dependent activities.
CA.dec: Winter city breaks can combine lights, cultural attractions and nearby snow activities. Ontario's tourism guidance stresses planning for winter driving and checking opening schedules and local conditions.

PT.nov: Portugal starts its transition into festive travel, with Óbidos's 2026 Christmas village opening in late November. Other towns run different schedules, so verify the chosen local programme.
PT.dec: Christmas traditions, seasonal food and markets shape city visits. Madeira's official 2026 programme begins December 1 and continues into January, culminating in New Year's Eve celebrations.

FR.nov: Paris's festive lights and shop windows begin appearing from mid-November. This city example supports cultural and shopping itineraries; other French regions have distinct seasonal programmes.
FR.dec: Christmas markets, illuminations, concerts and museum visits anchor Paris trips. Lyon's light festival adds a separate regional highlight; check opening hours around holidays and specific event dates.

GL.nov: A quieter Arctic month for northern lights, indoor arts and local culture. Polar darkness has begun in northern communities while southern towns retain short daylight. First Advent falls on November 29 in 2026; local tree-lighting arrangements need confirmation.
GL.dec: Christmas stars, community celebrations and small local fairs shape December. Northern towns experience polar darkness; Nuuk retains some daylight. Snow-dependent activities require local confirmation; many summer excursions do not run.

methodology.events: Primary-source major events, cultural celebrations and national commemorations, plus rule-based holiday calendars. Date status distinguishes confirmed 2026 programmes, fixed annual observances and unconfirmed seasonal records. Unknown dates are kept off the date grid. Selected-day events use their published opening-day arrays. Local events are not exhaustive.
methodology.flows: Country-specific source-market profiles and clearly separated2019 statistical references use historical periods, direction-specific definitions and primary sources. Selected countries have historical November/December monthly records. Archived World Bank/UN Tourism annual totals are shown separately and generally stop in 2020. They are not measured 2026 monthly demand, and accommodation arrivals, border crossings, trips, spending and nationalities are not interchangeable.
methodology.coverage: 250 country and territory records, including dependencies and disputed/reference areas. Polygon source is Natural Earth 1:50m. Small places also have centroid markers and are always available through search.
methodology.crawl: Travel-guide pages are automatically fetched and indexed. They provide background reading, not independently verified forecasts. Counted pages are distinct successfully retrieved URLs, not distinct websites.
methodology.seasonal: Seasonal notes describe broad patterns, not real-time conditions, booking volume or entry guidance.
methodology.license: Wikivoyage excerpts: CC BY-SA 4.0, attributed to linked page contributors. World geography: Natural Earth public domain; country metadata: mledoze/countries (ODbL); calendars: date-holidays (ISC). Community place descriptions adapted from Wikivoyage contributors are CC BY-SA4.0, with source revision and attribution per guide.  Archived tourism indicators: World Bank/UN Tourism, CC BY 4.0. Eurostat travel tables: European Commission reuse policy; definitions are stated per record.

indiaAudit.publication: India Tourism Statistics 2026, 67th edition, Ministry of Tourism, Government of India
indiaAudit.publisher: Research and Analytics Division, Ministry of Tourism
indiaAudit.originalDataSource: Bureau of Immigration, Government of India

comparison2024.description: Ministry of Tourism written Rajya Sabha reply, 7 August 2025; Bureau of Immigration country-wise annex

methodology.ranking: Descending count of individually reported country and territory rows in Annex A2.1 / A3.2. Region subtotals and the unallocated Others row excluded from ranking. Territories such as Hong Kong remain separate because the source reports them separately.
methodology.share: value / national annual total × 100, rounded to two decimal places. The published source share is preserved separately and may use coarser rounding.
methodology.outbound: Indian Nationals’ Departures are border departure movements by Indian nationals, across all recorded travel purposes. They are not unique Indian holidaymakers. One person can generate multiple departures. Destination country/territory is distinct from the traveller’s nationality.
methodology.inbound: Foreign Tourist Arrivals are India’s foreign-national arrival series, not state/city tourist visits and not the broader International Tourist Arrivals series that also includes non-resident Indian nationals.
methodology.leisure: Purpose shares are published country-level percentages for 2025. Estimated leisure departures multiply total departures by the rounded leisure percentage; these estimates are not separately published exact counts.
methodology.period: Annual 2025 history, not November/December 2026 measured flows or forecasts.

sourceConsistencyNotes: Country-level Annex A3.2 used for rankings and the 2024 comparison. Its 2024 United States, Thailand, Vietnam, Canada, Kuwait, Oman and Malaysia values agree with the August 2025 PIB country-wise release.

The summary Table 3.1.2 and nearby narrative contain inconsistent 2024 country/value pairings; the country annex is the evidence used here. In the verified country annex, Thailand moves from fourth in 2024 to third in 2025; the US moves from third to fourth.
The aggregate regional rows are excluded. The 2026 annex includes some apparent regional subtotal inconsistencies, so country rows are not replaced with regional summaries.

cityRanking.status: No comparable India-origin city visitation ranking verified across these destination markets.
cityRanking.note: A departure airport or arrival gateway is not a city visited. Generic destination highlights and holiday hubs must be labelled as suggestions, not India-specific visitor rankings. Country ranks cannot be applied to cities.

inbound.note: The individually reported inbound rows plus the published unclassified category are two arrivals below the published national total. Counts are preserved as printed; no allocation or correction is invented.

purposeOmissions.reason: The published purpose-table count differs from the country-annex count; purpose split withheld.

glossary.note: The glossary explicitly defines arrivals as visits rather than unique persons and states that repeated departures by Indian nationals are counted in the same way.

GL.title: Greenland city guide
GL.portRankingLabel: All 19 reported Greenland ports ranked by 2025 cruise passenger visits
GL.portRankingNote: The same passenger can visit several ports. Qassiarsuk is exempt from port charges, so reporting is incomplete there. City guide cards are selected examples, not the top five ports.
GL.description: Five practical bases with official destination guidance. These are places to visit within Greenland, not statistically ranked origin or outbound cities.

cities.description: Capital culture, museums, cafés and fjord scenery. A practical base for November–December with Christmas lights and local markets.

cities.name: Sisimiut
cities.description: Arctic Circle town with a large backcountry. The official guide places October–December in its quieter conference season; main dog-sled season is January–April.

cities.name: Qaqortoq
cities.description: South Greenland's harbour town, art and Norse heritage gateway. Most excursions run June–September; winter visitors should arrange services ahead.

cities.name: Tasiilaq
cities.description: East Greenland town reached through Kulusuk. Official guidance identifies February–April as its main winter activity season; November–December services need checking.

GL.cityMetricNote: Port visits can count the same cruise passenger in several towns. These are not unique people, hotel arrivals, resident outbound trips or November–December city demand.
GL.accessNote: Nuuk has year-round connections via Copenhagen and Keflavík. Qaqortoq's airport opened April 16, 2026. Route schedules indicate access, not where Greenland residents ultimately holiday.

cities.description: (Arabic: الجزائر) — The capital of Algeria, and the nation's political and cultural center. It is a vibrant and multicultural city, with a mix of French, Arab, and African influences. The city is well known for its beautiful architecture, stunning beaches, and lively nightlife.

cities.description: (Arabic: عنّابة) — a town with 200,000 inhabitants in the east of the country next to the border of Tunisia.

cities.name: Constantine
cities.description: (Arabic: قسنطينة) — Algeria's 3rd largest city with a canyon going down through it. Also known as "city of bridges" for having a lot of impressive and beautiful bridges.

cities.name: Oran
cities.description: (Arabic: وَهران) — Algeria's 2nd largest city after Algiers, also called "second Paris" or "Rai city " by Algerians, with many impressive buildings from colonial times and also being popular for making quality rai songs

cities.name: Sétif

cities.name: Tamanrasset

cities.description: The main cruise destination, with seas that support wildlife and are navigable in summer, and with the shortest crossing from temperate climates. The impressive heights of the Antarctic Andes and many research stations are here.

cities.name: Antarctic and sub-Antarctic islands
cities.description: These are widely separated across the wild Southern Ocean. The only ones routinely visited are the South Shetland Islands, but as these are close to the Antarctic Peninsula they're described there.

cities.name: East Antarctica
cities.description: This vast ice desert is seldom visited. But cruises to the Ross Sea sometimes follow the coast as far as Commonwealth Bay, where Mawson's Huts are the legacy of the 1911-13 expedition.

cities.name: West Antarctica
cities.description: This is barren and empty, with only a handful of research stations. But it does contain the continent's highest mountain, which you can climb on a guided expedition. You can also run a marathon here.

cities.name: Ross Sea
cities.description: Ross Island has the largest settlement on this continent, McMurdo Station. The island has several historic camp sites and Mount Erebus, an active volcano that you can climb. This is the usual destination for cruises from New Zealand or Australia.

cities.name: South Pole
cities.description: The furthest south you can go.

cities.name: Bridgetown
cities.description: The capital of Barbados and its suburbs are in Saint Michael Parish. The top attractions are the historic areas around the Careenage (old harbour) in city centre, and Garrison Savannah to the south which has the George Washington House. The city also hosts Mount Gay Rum Distilleries, Kensington Oval cricket ground, and the bases for scuba-diving…

cities.name: Western Barbados
cities.description: North of the city are the parishes of Saint James, Saint Peter and Saint Lucy. This is the west-facing, most sheltered coast, so it's the best for family beach holidays. Holetown and Speightstown are the two main townships, with many tourist hotels and small guesthouses along this strip.

cities.name: Southern Barbados
cities.description: The parish of Christ Church is a tourist strip of hotels, bars and restaurants, one long traffic jam honking its way through Rockley, Saint Lawrence (the main party zone), Oistins and Silver Sands. This south-facing coast is good both for water-based activities and family bathing. East of the airport is Saint Philip parish: this has fewer hotels,…

cities.name: Central Eastern Barbados
cities.description: The parishes of Saint Andrew, Saint George, Saint John, Saint Joseph and Saint Thomas are the least developed and most scenic part of the island. There are lush botanic gardens such as Andromeda, plantation houses such as Sunbury, and Harrison's Cave in the underlying limestone. The hilly east coast is exposed to the full fury of the Atlantic,…

cities.name: Elizabeth Castle
cities.description: Castle on a tidal islet, built from the 16th century when the stronghold at Mont Orgueil became vulnerable to improving cannon power. It was built over a confiscated abbey, and saw action during the English Civil Wars, and the Seven Years War with France. A barracks was also built, but the site made them sitting ducks so the garrison was moved to…

cities.name: Maritime Museum
cities.description: Great hands-on exposition of Jersey's colourful maritime history, which involved lots of pirates, privateers and other salty rapscallions. Includes the Occupation Tapestry Gallery commemorating wartime events.

cities.name: Jersey Museum & Art Gallery
cities.description: Interesting displays of Jersey life, from Ice Age hairy mammoths, farming and wildlife, Victoriana, the actress Lillie Langtry (1853-1929), and the Nazi occupation. Plus small art gallery.

cities.name: Samarès Manor Botanic Gardens
cities.description: The manor is medieval with Tudorbethan additions, now converted to self-catering flats. Samarès means salt marshes, and these were reclaimed in the 1920s to create the present gardens.

cities.name: Government House
cities.description: The official residence of the Lieutenant Governor of Jersey. Normally visitors are only permitted by official invitation (no, your Heritage Pass doesn't count), but they have very occasional open days.

cities.name: Ville-ès-Nouaux
cities.description: is a burial gallery and a dolmen set in a stone circle, from about 2500 BC. Its pottery was in the "Beaker" style of 2000 BC, widely found across Europe. Archaeologists blow hot and cold over whether this was made by a distinct "Beaker People", or was simply a popular style. The site is next to St Andrews Church and free.

cities.name: St Aubin's Fort
cities.description: stands on a tidal islet; it was built from the 16th century and periodically reinforced, including during the wartime occupation. It's reached by a causeway at low tide and is free to enter.

cities.name: Portelet Tower or Janvrin's Tomb
cities.description: on the tidal L'Île au Guerdain just off Portelet beach, is a stubby affair built in 1808 that never grew up into a Martello tower. cities.description: (Москва) — Russia's capital, one of the world's greatest cities and the 2nd biggest in Europe by population after Istanbul, has endless attractions to offer an adventurous visitor.

cities.name: Saint Petersburg
cities.description: (Санкт-Петербург) — Formerly called Leningrad, Russia's cultural and former imperial capital is home to the State Hermitage Museum, not only one of the world's finest museums, but also houses the 2nd largest art collection worldwide, while the city center is a living open-air museum in its own right, making this city one of the world's top travel…

cities.description: (Нижний Новгород) — Often overlooked despite being one of the largest cities in Russia, Nizhny Novgorod is well worth a visit for its Kremlin, the Andrey Sakharov Museum, and nearby Makaryev Monastery.

cities.name: Sochi
cities.description: (Сочи) — Russia's favorite Black Sea beach resort, which was a favourite vacation spot of Stalin, was largely unknown to foreigners until it hosted the 2014 Winter Olympic Games.

cities.name: Vladivostok
cities.description: (Владивосток) — Often called "Russia's San Francisco" for its hilly streets and battleships. This port city is Russia's principal hub on the Pacific, and is the terminus of the Trans-Siberian Highway and Trans-Siberian Railway.

cities.name: Volgograd
cities.description: (Волгоград) — Formerly called Stalingrad, this city was the scene of perhaps the deciding battle of the European theatre of World War II, and now home to a massive war memorial, situated within Mamayev Kurgan.

cities.name: Yekaterinburg
cities.description: (Екатеринбург) — The center of the Urals region and one of Russia's principal cultural centers, it is a good stop on the Trans-Siberian Railway and an arrival point for visitors to the Urals, the second Russian financial center, and the place where the last Tsar and his family were executed by the Bolsheviks.

cities.name: Willis Island
cities.description: is accessible only by a hazardous landing onto a rocky cliff, followed by a steep ascent over rock and through tussocks. It's home to massive numbers of black-browed, grey-headed and light-mantled sooty albatross, as well as macaroni penguins. The islet just east is Vaughan Island, the larger one east is Trinity, then the little ones further east…

cities.name: Bird Island
cities.description: is a research area for the British Antarctic Survey and you may not land. The birds include wandering albatross and giant petrels.

cities.name: Elsehul
cities.description: is a mainland cove where it's almost impossible to land Dec / Jan with the vast numbers of grumpy fur seals that overrun the beaches. At other times of the year it's home to elephant seals, gentoo penguins, king penguins, sheathbills, and grey-headed albatross.

cities.name: Right Whale Bay
cities.description: is a bight on the north coast where cruise ships often stop. The Southern Right Whale Eubalaena australis is baleen, a filter feeder, and got its name because it was "the right whale to hunt" - hence the island's stations. Elephant seals and a small colony of king penguins throng the area Sept-Nov then thousands of fur seals take over the beach…

cities.name: Salisbury Plain
cities.description: is another enormous king penguin rookery, and hosts vast numbers of other penguins and seals.

cities.name: Leith Harbour
cities.description: or Port Leith is an abandoned whaling station within Stromness Bay, in operation 1905-1965. It was established by Christian Salvesen Ltd, and named for their home port in Edinburgh. In 1982 it ignited the Falklands War when 50 Argentines landed, supposedly contractors come to remove scrap metal from the old station; but they arrived mob-handed and…

cities.name: St Andrew's Bay
cities.description: has astronomical numbers of king penguins, plus thousands of elephant seals and fur seals occupying the sands along the water. The sights, sounds and smells of this bay will not soon be forgotten.

cities.name: Cooper Bay
cities.description: sheltered (somewhat) by Cooper Island, has South Georgia's most accessible macaroni penguin colony.

travelReferenceMetadata.provider: Derived basic statistical references from World Tourism Organization (UNWTO), Yearbook of Tourism Statistics2023, data2017–2021
travelReferenceMetadata.methodology: Newly calculated leading-country reference lists from2019 factual observations. Source prose, layout, regional aggregates and complete source tables are not reproduced. Original yearbook tables have different populations; their definitions are retained. Full coordinate extract stays work-only. Outbound references use ONLY one-year table1 border tourist arrivals by residence and are explicitly partial destination-reported samples.

travelStatsMetadata.provider: World Bank, World Development Indicators; underlying source UN Tourism
travelStatsMetadata.scope: Archived annual international tourism indicators. The source series stops in 2020, and some countries last reported earlier. These are annual trips and monetary totals, not unique people, bilateral rankings or November/December 2026 demand. The pandemic strongly affects 2020; 2019 is shown separately as a pre-pandemic reference.
